title: Sen. Al Cutrona voted Yea on SB419, a temporary instruction permit eligibility bill
text:
Sen. Al Cutrona voted Yea on SB419, a temporary instruction permit eligibility bill
Sen. Al Cutrona (R-33rd) voted Yea on SB419, a temporary instruction permit eligibility bill, which passed the Ohio Senate 33-0 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill lowers the minimum age to obtain a temporary instruction permit for a driver's license from 15 1/2 to 15 and requires juveniles to hold that permit for at least one year, instead of six months, before becoming eligible for a probationary license. It keeps existing conditions for supervised driving, nighttime driving restrictions and seat belt requirements, as well as limits on passengers for probationary license holders. The bill appears intended to let youths start supervised driving earlier while extending the learning period before unsupervised driving.
SB419 was introduced by Sen. Theresa Gavarone.
Cutrona represents the 33rd Ohio Senate District and was appointed to the Ohio Senate in 2024.
He previously served two terms in the Ohio House, where he chaired the Health Provider Services Committee and sponsored House Bill 2, the state capital budget.
Cutrona earned his bachelor's degree in Political Science and History from Youngstown State University, graduating cum laude.
He also holds a J.D. from Case Western Reserve University School of Law, where he received a leadership scholarship and completed a clerkship with the Ohio Seventh District Court of Appeals.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
